chapterBreakdown.gentle: Some of the patterns in this book play themselves out in a single conversation. Life games are different. They are biographical. They run for years, organize the player's whole working life, and end the same way every time even though the names at the top of the contract or the names on the colleagues' badges keep changing. Greta has been signing the same business partnership since her twenties. Felix has been collecting his colleagues' procedural lapses for twenty years and releasing them on a schedule. Ivar has been blaming the nearest witness for any mistake. A fourth player has been taking on more work than can be completed and proving the problem is structural. The shape is the same in all of them. The previous chapters' tools still apply. The only thing that changes is the time horizon, and the time horizon is the part most readers get wrong.

They are the patterns that run for years or decades, with the same opening move, the same predictable counter, and the same payoff distributed across whole working lives. The four-part anatomy and the stickiness equation from earlier chapters apply directly to all four. The new claim is the time horizon. That is the only genuinely new idea the chapter introduces. The antithesis to a life game is not a single conversation. It is a multi-year project requiring a new stroke supply and a slow update of the position, and the chapter is honest about that scale because dishonesty about the scale is the most common reason readers conclude the model does not work.

The shape is recognizable across very different players: same opening move, same counter, same switch, same payoff, distributed across years. The leverage in the chapter is the time horizon. The antithesis to a thirty-year pattern is not a conversation. It is a project requiring a new stroke supply and a slow update of the position that the pattern has been confirming for years. chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Most of the patterns the previous chapters described run in a single conversation, or a single relationship, or at most a single recurring weekly meeting or setting. Life games are different. They run on a biographical scale: years, sometimes whole decades. The same opening move, the same predictable response, the same switch, the same payoff, distributed across the player's entire working life.

Greta is sitting at a coffee table signing the fourth partnership agreement of her career. Each of the previous three partnerships ended the same way: a partner who was generous and excited at signing turned out, six months in, to take more than their share. Greta describes each ending as bad luck. The fourth one is going to end the same way because the pattern is not luck. The thesis of her game is exploitability: she makes herself easy to take from, somebody takes, and the position she has been holding since her twenties (the world will take what it can take) is confirmed one more time. The strokes are the small reliable acknowledgment of being seen as generous and put-upon afterward. The dynamics are her need for the position to stay confirmed.

Felix is the head of a department at a regional hospital and runs a different pattern. He has been collecting his colleagues' procedural lapses in a private file for years, then waiting for one of them to make an unambiguous mistake before releasing the stored anger of all the previous lapses as a justified, technically-correct response. The thesis is the collection plus the release. The antithesis is a colleague who is so impeccable in their work that Felix's file stays empty. The dynamics are Felix's need to keep the position confirmed that he is the only one in the room with standards. The payoff is the moral charge of guilt-free anger plus the strokes of being feared as the standards-keeper. The chapter does not use Berne's name for this pattern. The structure is the lesson.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Berne placed life games at the deepest level of his catalog because they are the longest-running cases the model handles. They are biographical, not local: they run on a multi-year schedule, organizing the player's whole working life. The same opening move, the same predictable response, the same switch, the same payoff, distributed across years rather than across an afternoon.

The chapter walks through four patterns. The exploitability pattern is Greta's: she signs a generous business partnership, makes herself easy to take from, gets taken from, and describes the ending as bad luck. The position confirmed is that the world takes what it can. The righteous-outrage pattern is Felix's: a department head who collects his colleagues' procedural lapses for months and then releases the stored anger as a justified, technically-correct response. The position confirmed is that he is the only one in the room with standards. The displaced-blame pattern is Ivar's: a project coordinator who explains every mistake on every project as the consequence of the colleague who interrupted him at the critical moment. The position confirmed is that he never causes the things that go wrong. He has worked in the same coordinator role at three different organizations and the pattern has run identically at all three, down to the same timing and the same switching move. A fourth pattern is Mona's, which shares structural features with both Greta's and Ivar's: she takes on more work than she can complete at rates she cannot sustain, then proves nothing can be done about it. Each new client confirms the position: the demands are real, the time is genuinely short, and the arrangement could not have worked.

All four have the four-part anatomy from the third chapter and the stickiness equation from the fourth, applied at biographical scale. The new claim, and the only one this chapter actually cares about, is the time horizon. The antithesis to a life game is not a single conversation. It is a multi-year project requiring a new stroke supply and a slow update of the position the pattern has been confirming for decades.

Felix is the head of a department at a regional hospital and has been collecting procedural lapses from his colleagues for twenty years, releasing them on a schedule of his own as justified, technically-correct outrage. Ivar is a project coordinator who has been explaining every mistake as the fault of the colleague who interrupted him at the critical moment. Mona is a freelancer who has been taking on more work than she can complete at rates she cannot sustain for ten years and proving nothing can be done about it. Each new client confirms it in the same way.

All four have the four-part anatomy from the third chapter and the stickiness equation from the fourth, distributed across years instead of conversations. A reader who watches Greta's antithesis-partner refuse to exploit her, and watches Greta find another partner who will, has watched the model do exactly what the model is supposed to do at the right time scale. chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The previous four chapters built the tools for reading a single conversation, a single transaction, a single recurring pattern, and the energetics that keep the recurring pattern sticky. This chapter takes those tools to the deepest cases the model handles: the patterns that organize the player's whole working life, distributed across years and decades rather than across conversations. Berne called them life games and placed them first in the catalog because every later catalog chapter is a smaller, faster version of the same machinery.

Greta is sitting at a coffee table signing her fourth partnership agreement. Each of the previous three ended the same way. The thesis of her pattern is exploitability: she is genuinely generous, genuinely available, and genuinely not protective of what she offers, and over the course of a six-month partnership the partner will find the ways she has made herself easy to take from and will take. The antithesis would be a partner who declines to take, treats her generously, and watches Greta find another partner who will. The dynamics are Greta's need for the position she has been holding since her twenties to keep getting confirmed. The payoff is the proof that the world takes what it can, plus the small reliable strokes of being seen as the generous one afterward.

Felix is the head of a department at a regional hospital. He runs a different pattern. He has been collecting his colleagues' procedural lapses in a small private file for twenty years, then waiting for one of them to make an unambiguous mistake before releasing the stored anger of all the previous lapses as a justified, technically-correct response. The position confirmed is that he is the only one in the room with standards. The payoff is the moral charge of guilt-free anger and the strokes of being feared as the standards-keeper. The antithesis is a colleague who is so impeccably procedural that Felix's file stays empty. Ivar is in a third pattern: a project coordinator who explains every mistake as the consequence of the colleague who interrupted him at the critical moment. Mona, in a fourth, is a freelancer who has been taking on more work than she can complete at rates she cannot sustain for ten years.

The chapter's hardest claim is about the time horizon. The antithesis to a life game is not a sentence. It is a project. A reader who watches Greta's antithesis-partner decline to exploit her and expects Greta to leave the pattern in the next month is using the right model on the wrong time scale. Greta cannot leave the pattern in a month, because the pattern has been paying her strokes she has not built another source for and confirming a position she has been holding since her twenties, and both have to be replaced before the pattern becomes possible to leave. The chapter is honest about this because dishonesty about the time horizon is the most common reason readers conclude the model is broken when it is not.

They are biographical rather than local: they run on a multi-year schedule and organize the player's whole working life. The previous chapters' tools (state observation, single-transaction vector, four-part anatomy, stickiness equation) all apply, on a much longer time horizon than the reader is likely expecting.

The chapter walks through four patterns from the original taxonomy as worked examples. The first is the exploitability pattern. Greta runs a small graphic design studio and is about to sign the fourth partnership agreement of her career. The previous three ended the same way: she made herself easy to take from, somebody took, and the position she has been holding since her twenties got confirmed one more time. The antithesis would be a partner who declined to take and treated her generously, and Greta would find another partner who would. The dynamics are her need for the position to be confirmed. The payoff is the confirmation plus the small reliable strokes of being seen as generous and put-upon.

The second is the righteous-outrage pattern. Felix is the head of a department at a regional hospital. He has been collecting his colleagues' procedural lapses in a private file for twenty years and releasing them, on a schedule of his own, as justified, technically-correct outrage when one of them eventually makes an unambiguous mistake. The position confirmed is I'm OK and you're not. The payoff is the moral charge of guilt-free anger plus the strokes of being feared as the standards-keeper. The antithesis is impeccable procedure that gives Felix no opening at all.

The third is the displaced-blame pattern. Ivar is a project coordinator who has been explaining every mistake on every project as the consequence of the colleague who interrupted him at the critical moment. The antithesis is the colleague who refuses to accept the blame, calmly, with the actual timeline in their hand. The dynamics are Ivar's avoidance of a position he cannot hold in front of himself. The payoff is the elimination of the mistake from his ledger. A fourth pattern is Mona's: a freelancer who takes on work she cannot complete at rates she cannot sustain, runs the drama of near-misses for several months, and collects sympathy strokes when the work fails.

Two structural facts must travel together into hard depth. The first is that the four-part anatomy and the stickiness equation apply directly to all four patterns. The second is that the time horizon is the part the reader is most likely to get wrong. The antithesis to a life game is years of replacement work plus a slow update of the life position the pattern has been confirming. A reader who applies the third chapter's antithesis at a five-minute horizon to a multi-year pattern will see no results, and the time horizon is the only thing that has to change.

point.gentle: Worth sitting with: at biographical scale, the antithesis is not a conversation. It is a multi-year project requiring a new stroke supply and a position update.
point.direct: At biographical scale, the antithesis is not a conversation. It is a multi-year project requiring a new stroke supply and a position update.
point.competitive: At biographical scale, the antithesis is not a conversation. It is a multi-year project requiring a new stroke supply and a position update. This is non-negotiable.

moreDetails.gentle: Notice this: greta cannot leave the exploitability pattern in a month because the pattern has been paying her strokes she has not built another source for and confirming a position she has been holding since her twenties. Both have to be replaced before the pattern becomes possible to leave. A reader who applies the third chapter's antithesis at a five-minute horizon to a multi-year pattern will see no results, and the time horizon is the part most readers use wrong.
moreDetails.direct: Greta cannot leave the exploitability pattern in a month because the pattern has been paying her strokes she has not built another source for and confirming a position she has been holding since her twenties. Both have to be replaced before the pattern becomes possible to leave. A reader who applies the third chapter's antithesis at a five-minute horizon to a multi-year pattern will see no results, and the time horizon is the part most readers use wrong.
moreDetails.competitive: Greta cannot leave the exploitability pattern in a month because the pattern has been paying her strokes she has not built another source for and confirming a position she has been holding since her twenties. Both have to be replaced before the pattern becomes possible to leave. A reader who applies the third chapter's antithesis at a five-minute horizon to a multi-year pattern will see no results, and the time horizon is the part most readers use wrong. Know this cold.

activationPrompt.gentle: Think of a multi-year painful pattern you have either watched or run yourself, and try to walk it through the four-part anatomy from the previous chapter (thesis, antithesis, dynamics, payoff) and the stickiness equation from the chapter before (strokes plus life position). The shape should be visible by the end of the walk.
activationPrompt.direct: Walk a multi-year pattern in your own life through the four-part anatomy and the stickiness equation. Be specific about each of the six components. If you cannot specify them, you have not yet seen the pattern at biographical scale.
activationPrompt.competitive: Walk a multi-year pattern through the four-part anatomy and the stickiness equation. Six components, specific. If any of the six are vague, you are still seeing the surface and not the structure.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: When did you most recently catch yourself reconstructing a recurring painful instance from your own life and notice that you have described it before, in identical words, to the same friends?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Name the most recent time you reconstructed a painful instance from your life and noticed the reconstruction was identical to a previous one. What did you do with the recognition?
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Find the most recent identical reconstruction of a painful instance you have had. The identical reconstruction is the diagnosis. What you did or did not do with it is the data about whether you are running the pattern or watching it run you.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: Where in your immediate circle is there a long-running life game in which you are a member of the cast (rescuer, witness, or other supporting role), and what would the cost be of refusing your role even once?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Identify a life game in your immediate circle in which you are a member of the cast (not the player). Name your role specifically and estimate the cost of refusing it once.
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Name the life game in your circle in which you are the supporting cast. Identify your role. Estimate the cost of refusing it. The cost is what has been keeping you in the cast.

predictionPrompt.gentle: If, for the next year, you slowly built one positive stroke source per month outside the rooms where the multi-year patterns in your life have been running, what do you predict you would notice in the eleventh and twelfth months?
predictionPrompt.direct: Predict what would change in a multi-year pattern in your life if you spent twelve months building one new positive stroke source per month outside the rooms where the pattern lives. Be specific about what would shift and what would not.
predictionPrompt.competitive: Run the experiment in your head: twelve months, one new positive stroke source per month, all outside the rooms where the multi-year pattern has been running. What would the pattern look like in month twelve? What would still be in place?

retrieve.gentle: Worth understanding: four life-game patterns at biographical scale: the exploitability pattern (Greta), the righteous-outrage pattern (Felix), the displaced-blame pattern (Ivar), and the over-commit pattern (Mona). Each is a worked example of the four-part anatomy and the stickiness equation at multi-year scale. The antithesis is a multi-year project requiring a new stroke supply and a slow position update.
retrieve.direct: Four life-game patterns at biographical scale: the exploitability pattern (Greta), the righteous-outrage pattern (Felix), the displaced-blame pattern (Ivar), and the over-commit pattern (Mona). Each is a worked example of the four-part anatomy and the stickiness equation at multi-year scale. The antithesis is a multi-year project requiring a new stroke supply and a slow position update.
retrieve.competitive: Four life-game patterns at biographical scale: the exploitability pattern (Greta), the righteous-outrage pattern (Felix), the displaced-blame pattern (Ivar), and the over-commit pattern (Mona). Each is a worked example of the four-part anatomy and the stickiness equation at multi-year scale. The antithesis is a multi-year project requiring a new stroke supply and a slow position update. This is the foundation.

connect.gentle: Notice this: the chapter applies the previous four chapters' tools (state observation, single-transaction vector, four-part anatomy, stickiness equation) to the longest-arc cases the model handles. The new claim is about time horizon, not about new tools.
connect.direct: The chapter applies the previous four chapters' tools (state observation, single-transaction vector, four-part anatomy, stickiness equation) to the longest-arc cases the model handles. The new claim is about time horizon, not about new tools.
connect.competitive: The chapter applies the previous four chapters' tools (state observation, single-transaction vector, four-part anatomy, stickiness equation) to the longest-arc cases the model handles. The new claim is about time horizon, not about new tools. Know this cold.

preview.gentle: Consider carefully: life games are biographical and slow. The next chapter takes the same machinery to the much narrower scale of two people who have agreed to share a life, where the time horizon is shorter and the per-move stakes are higher.
preview.direct: Life games are biographical and slow. The next chapter takes the same machinery to the much narrower scale of two people who have agreed to share a life, where the time horizon is shorter and the per-move stakes are higher.
preview.competitive: Life games are biographical and slow. The next chapter takes the same machinery to the much narrower scale of two people who have agreed to share a life, where the time horizon is shorter and the per-move stakes are higher. Internalize this now.

examples.title: Felix springs the trap on Rafa

scenario.gentle: Tuesday morning. Felix's office at the regional hospital. Felix has been waiting for this conversation for two weeks, since Rafa filed the wrong billing code on the Whitfield case. Felix knew about the wrong code the day it was filed. He has not said anything until this morning, because he needed Rafa to make one more error before the conversation could be the conversation Felix wanted to have. Rafa knocks. Felix tells him to sit down. The two-week file is in Felix's desk drawer.
scenario.direct: FELIX (department head, twenty years in, file in drawer): Rafa, sit down. We need to talk about the Whitfield billing. RAFA (longest-serving colleague): Yes? FELIX (releasing two weeks of stored anger as one justified sentence): The billing code on the Whitfield case was wrong. So was the one on the Pereira case last month. So was the intake form on the Castro case in August. The structure is the spring of the trap. Felix is technically right about each item. The release is the payoff.
scenario.competitive: Felix knew about the Whitfield billing error the day it was filed. He waited two weeks. He was waiting for the next thing, because the next thing was the procedural moment that would let him release the stored anger of the Pereira case from last month and the Castro case from August at the same time, all at once, all justified, all technically correct. When Rafa knocked on his door this Tuesday morning, Felix had the file ready. The conversation Felix had been waiting for was not about the billing. The billing was the trigger. The release was the payoff.

whatToDo.gentle: If you find yourself in Rafa's seat, the first move is not to defend yourself or apologize. It is to ask for the items in writing. 'Felix, I want to make sure I understand each of these. Can you send them to me in an email so I can address them properly?' The written list defangs the release.
whatToDo.direct: Ask for the items in writing before responding to any of them. 'Send me the list, Felix. I will respond to each one individually.' The written request interrupts the release because the release depends on the in-person delivery and the cumulative outrage, neither of which survives a written list answered point by point.
whatToDo.competitive: One sentence: 'Send me each item in writing and I will respond to them individually.' That sentence is the antithesis at the small scale. It refuses the role of the witness to the release and converts the cumulative outrage into a list of specific procedural items, each of which can be addressed alone, and the cumulative charge dissipates.

whyItMatters.gentle: The righteous-outrage pattern lives in the in-person release. Converting the release into a written list of items addressed individually is the cleanest way to interrupt the pattern without confronting the person running it.
whyItMatters.direct: The pattern's payoff is the cumulative release in person. Converting it to a written list addressed point by point removes the cumulative charge and the in-person audience, both of which are essential to the pattern's payoff.
whyItMatters.competitive: Written list, addressed individually, no audience. That is the structural defense against the righteous-outrage pattern, and it is the only one that does not require the colleague to confront the player. It is the cheapest exit from the cast role.

examples.title: Mona in the second week of November

scenario.gentle: It is the second week of November and I am in the middle of cycle eleven, or twelve, of the same thing I have been doing for ten years. I took on three projects last month from three different clients at rates I knew were too low when I quoted them, and I am now working ten-hour days I cannot sustain trying to make all three of them ship before the holidays, knowing that one of them is going to slip and that the slip is going to be the moment I get to tell my closest friends, with full justification, that nothing can be done about my situation. I am noticing, this November, that I have been doing this since I started freelancing.
scenario.direct: First-person, second week of November, middle of cycle. Three projects taken on at unsustainable rates last month. Ten-hour days. The slip is going to come around the second week of December and the sympathy will follow. I have been doing this for ten years. The payoff is not the work shipping; it is the proof that nothing can be done about my situation. I have not noticed this before this week.
scenario.competitive: Cycle eleven, second week of November. Three projects at rates I knew were too low when I signed. Ten-hour days. I have been doing this since I started freelancing. The slip in December is going to be the moment I get to tell my closest friends, fully justified, that the situation is impossible. That moment is what I have been working toward for ten years. The work is not the work. The proof is the work.

whatToDo.gentle: When you catch yourself in cycle eleven of a pattern you have been running for years, the move is not to make this cycle different by force. It is to write down, this week, exactly what each cycle has been paying you. The writing is the entire intervention. Trying to make this cycle the better one will fail, because the pattern is paying you something the work itself is not.
whatToDo.direct: Write down what each cycle has been paying you. Specifically. Not 'sympathy' but 'sympathy from these three friends, in this rhythm, on this schedule.' The specificity is what makes the next cycle different. Trying to make the work itself succeed misses the payoff entirely.
whatToDo.competitive: Specific. Not 'sympathy.' Names, frequencies, the exact texture of what the cycle has been paying. Until you can write that down honestly, the next cycle will be cycle twelve, identical to cycle eleven and to all the cycles before it. The specificity of the writing is the only intervention that matters this month.

whyItMatters.gentle: Self-employed people running multi-year over-commit patterns are quietly common and quietly miserable. The intervention is not better project selection. It is honest specificity about what the pattern has been paying.
whyItMatters.direct: Over-commit patterns in freelance work are stroke-economy patterns wearing a financial costume. The intervention is honest specificity about what each cycle has been paying, not better project management.
whyItMatters.competitive: A freelancer who can write down honestly what each ten-year cycle has been paying them has options the unaware version of themselves does not. The unaware version will run cycle twelve next year and cycle twenty in 2034, and the project management will not change either of those.

examples.title: Tomi in Mr. Wendell's history class

scenario.gentle: Tomi is a high school junior in Mr. Wendell's history class. Tomi has spent the semester arriving late to discussion sections, choosing the wrong tone in class with the wrong students, and then reacting with quiet astonishment when his classmates and his teachers respond exactly the way the choices were inviting them to respond. Wendell has watched the pattern long enough to recognize it. He also knows that calling Tomi out for it directly will not help and will probably make Tomi run a slightly louder version of it next week.
scenario.direct: Wendell's history classroom, third quarter. Tomi (junior) has been arriving late to discussion, using the wrong tone with the wrong classmates, then reacting with surprised hurt when the predictable responses arrive. Wendell has tracked the pattern for two months. Direct confrontation will worsen it. A structural intervention is required, and the structural intervention has to come from a place that does not punish.
scenario.competitive: Tomi has been running the same shape in Wendell's history classroom since September. Late, wrong tone, surprised hurt at the consequences, sympathy from the small group of friends who comfort him afterward. Wendell has tracked it long enough to know that the pattern is paying Tomi the sympathy on a schedule, that the pattern is confirming a position Tomi has been holding since middle school, and that any direct confrontation will make Tomi run a louder version of it next week. The intervention has to come from somewhere the pattern is not.

whatToDo.gentle: Wendell does not call Tomi out. He gives Tomi a small, specific responsibility in the next class that has nothing to do with the pattern. He asks Tomi to lead the small-group discussion on Thursday. The responsibility is the structural intervention; it gives Tomi a different stroke source for that one class period that is not the sympathy after a misstep.
whatToDo.direct: Give Tomi a small, specific responsibility in the next session that has nothing to do with the pattern. Lead a small group, present a passage, run an in-class poll. The responsibility is a stroke source that does not require the misstep, and it interrupts the pattern at the structural level rather than the punitive level.
whatToDo.competitive: One small specific responsibility, in the next class, that pays a stroke for a different reason. Lead the small group on Thursday. Present the opening passage on Monday. The responsibility is a different stroke source for the same class period, and it competes structurally with the pattern. Direct confrontation does not. Punishment does not. A different source does.

whyItMatters.gentle: Adolescent rejection-inviting patterns are easy to misread as bad behavior and almost never respond to punishment. The structural intervention (a different stroke source in the same setting) is the only thing that has a chance.
whyItMatters.direct: Adolescent rejection-inviting patterns are stroke economies. They respond to alternative stroke sources, not to punishment or direct confrontation. A teacher who can offer the alternative source in the same setting is the only intervention that scales.
whyItMatters.competitive: A teacher who can give a rejection-seeking adolescent a different stroke source in the same room they are running the pattern in has changed the pattern. Punishment confirms the pattern. Confrontation confirms the pattern. Different source replaces the pattern.

examples.title: Wendell coaches Sora in the staff room

scenario.gentle: Wendell is sitting with Sora, a new teacher at his school, in the staff room after Friday classes. Sora has just had her first hard week with a student named Tomi who is running the same pattern Wendell has been watching for two semesters. Sora is new and is treating it the way new teachers treat it: directly, with consequences. Wendell knows the consequences will not work. He has to give Sora the structural read without making her feel like the consequences were stupid.
scenario.direct: Wendell's staff room conversation with Sora (new teacher, first hard week with Tomi's pattern). Sora has been responding to the pattern with consequences: detentions, written warnings, parent calls. Wendell knows the consequences will not work because the pattern is paying Tomi the sympathy strokes the consequences generate. He has to hand Sora the structural reading without making her feel her instincts were wrong.
scenario.competitive: Sora has been giving Tomi consequences for two weeks and the consequences are making the pattern louder. Wendell can see this. Sora cannot, yet, because the consequences are the obvious response and her instinct is correct in nine out of ten classroom situations. Wendell has eight minutes in the staff room before the bus, and his job is to hand Sora the structural read without telling her that her instincts were wrong, because they were not wrong, they were the wrong tool for this specific case.

whatToDo.gentle: Wendell asks Sora a question instead of telling her the answer. 'What does Tomi look like in the twenty minutes after he gets the consequence?' Then he waits. Sora will say something about how Tomi has friends who comfort him, or that he gets quiet, or that he leaves the room. Whichever she says, Wendell can use to hand her the diagnosis: 'That is what the pattern is paying him.'
whatToDo.direct: Ask Sora what Tomi looks like in the twenty minutes after the consequence. Wait for the answer. The answer will reveal the stroke source. Then say: 'That is what the pattern is paying him, and it is what the consequence is delivering on a schedule.' The diagnosis lands because Sora has produced it from her own observation.
whatToDo.competitive: Question first. 'What does Tomi look like twenty minutes after the detention?' Sora will name the stroke source herself. Then: 'That is what your detention is paying him.' The sentence is short because the diagnosis has to be in Sora's hands by the end of it, and her instincts have to remain unbruised because she will need them in the next nine cases this semester.

whyItMatters.gentle: Coaching new teachers on rejection-seeking patterns without making them feel their consequences were stupid is the harder version of the structural reading. The question-first approach lets the new teacher produce the diagnosis themselves.
whyItMatters.direct: Mid-career teachers coaching new teachers on stroke-economy patterns have to preserve the new teacher's instincts about consequences (which are usually correct) while introducing the structural read for the specific cases where consequences fail. The question-first approach is the only one that does both.
whyItMatters.competitive: A new teacher who is told her consequences are wrong will lose confidence in consequences for the next year. A new teacher who produces the structural read herself, in the staff room, with help, will keep her consequences for the cases that need them and add the structural read for the cases that do not. The question-first approach is the only one that preserves both.

scenario.gentle: Late on a Wednesday night, Greta sat at her kitchen table with the new contract on top and walked backwards through her three previous partnerships. The third one was with Marcellus, who had taken a generous share of the credit on the rebrand work. The second one was with Yael, who had taken a generous share of the cash on the editorial project. The first one was with Sasha, who had taken both. Greta noticed, this Wednesday night, that she had described all three of these endings to her closest friends as bad luck, and that the descriptions had been word-for-word identical, and that the new contract under her hand was about to start the same arc again with someone whose name was different and whose face was different and whose generosity at the signing was the same.
scenario.direct: Wednesday night, Greta's kitchen table, three previous partnerships reconstructed in order. Marcellus on the rebrand: took the credit. Yael on the editorial: took the cash. Sasha on the original studio launch: took both. Greta has described all three endings as bad luck in word-for-word identical sentences to her closest friends. The fourth contract is on the table. The shape is now unmistakable to her, for the first time, and it is not yet clear whether the recognition will change anything.
scenario.competitive: Three partnerships reconstructed at the kitchen table on a Wednesday night. Sasha at the launch, who took everything. Yael on the editorial project, who took the cash. Marcellus on the rebrand, who took the credit. Greta has been describing all three of these endings to the same three friends in the same words for years, and Wednesday night is the first time she has noticed that the descriptions are identical. The fourth contract is under her hand. The shape is now visible. What is not yet visible is whether tonight's recognition is going to be different from the previous three reconstructions she has done at this table.

whatToDo.gentle: When you reconstruct the previous instances of a pattern and find them identical, the move is not to tear up the next contract. It is to write down, on the same page as the reconstruction, what the previous endings were paying you. Specifically. The writing is the first move; the contract decision is downstream of the writing.
whatToDo.direct: Write what the previous endings were paying you on the same page as the reconstruction. Specifically: which friend, which conversation, which words, which feeling. The specificity converts the recognition into something durable. The contract decision can wait until the writing is done.
whatToDo.competitive: Same page, both halves: the reconstruction on the top, what each ending paid you on the bottom. Names, conversations, the exact texture. Anything less specific will not survive the night, and the recognition will fade by Friday. The contract decision is not the move. The writing is.

whyItMatters.gentle: Late-night reconstructions of long-running patterns are common and almost never durable past the next morning. The on-page writing of what each instance was paying is the only intervention that survives the night.
whyItMatters.direct: The reconstruction itself is not the intervention. The on-page accounting of what each instance was paying is. Without the accounting, the reconstruction will fade by morning and the next instance will run identically.
whyItMatters.competitive: Reconstructions without on-page accounting are catharsis, not intervention. The accounting is what survives the morning. Without it, the next contract will be signed and the next ending will be described in the same identical words to the same three friends.

scenario.gentle: It is three hours after the project review meeting where I told everyone that the missed deadline was because Zoe had asked me about the client preferences at 2pm on Wednesday. Zoe did not ask me about the client preferences at 2pm on Wednesday. Zoe asked me a different question, about a different client, three days earlier, and the missed deadline had nothing to do with her question or with any other interruption that week. I am sitting at my desk at 6pm and I am thinking about the sentence I said in the meeting and I am noticing, for the first time in eleven years of doing this, that the sentence was a sentence I have used before with a different colleague's name in it.
scenario.direct: 6pm at Ivar's desk, three hours after the project review meeting. The sentence I said in the meeting was 'Zoe asked me about the client preferences at 2pm Wednesday and I lost my train of thought.' The sentence is not true. I have used a structurally identical sentence in the last four project reviews, with four different colleagues' names in it. I am noticing this for the first time. The decision in front of me is whether to walk to Zoe's desk before she leaves and tell her the sentence was not true, or to let it stand.
scenario.competitive: Three hours after the project review meeting, 6pm, my desk. The sentence about Zoe and the 2pm Wednesday interruption was not true and I knew it was not true when I said it and the people in the meeting heard it land and I am now noticing that I have said a structurally identical sentence in each of the last four project reviews with a different colleague's name in it each time. Zoe is still here. The decision in front of me is about thirty seconds wide. Walk to her desk and say the sentence was wrong, or let it stand and use it again next quarter with a different name in it.

whatToDo.gentle: When you catch yourself in the act of having just run an alibi pattern, the first move is not to confess publicly. It is to walk, privately, to the colleague whose name was in the alibi and say one specific sentence. 'What I said about you in the meeting about the deadline was not accurate, and I wanted you to know directly.' That is the entire move. The public correction can come later or not at all; the private one is the structural intervention.
whatToDo.direct: Walk to the colleague's desk. One sentence: 'What I said about you in the meeting was not accurate.' Do not elaborate. Do not justify. The sentence is the antithesis at the personal scale. Public correction is downstream and is not the first move.
whatToDo.competitive: Walk to her desk. One sentence: 'What I said about you in that meeting was not accurate, and I wanted you to know.' Anything longer will sound like a justification. Anything shorter will sound like nothing. Do it before she leaves. Do not do it tomorrow. Tomorrow is when the recognition fades and the pattern wins again.

whyItMatters.gentle: The displaced-blame pattern lives in the gap between the meeting and the private follow-up that almost never happens. The single private sentence to the named colleague is the intervention.
whyItMatters.direct: The pattern's payoff depends on the public alibi standing without correction. A private one-sentence correction to the named colleague removes the payoff retroactively and is the only intervention that survives the cycle.
whyItMatters.competitive: A single private sentence to the colleague whose name was in the alibi removes the payoff. The public version of the correction is much harder and not necessary. The private one is the structural antithesis, and it is the only one that has a chance of doing the actual work the chapter is recommending.

questions.prompt: What feature distinguishes a life game from the kind of recurring game the previous chapters described?
choices: A life game involves more dramatic content
A life game runs at biographical scale: the same opening move, counter, switch, and payoff distributed across years rather than across a single conversation
A life game involves a larger cast of people

explanation.gentle: Time horizon and biographical scope are the structural difference. The previous chapters dealt with games inside single conversations or single relationships; life games organize whole working lives. Drama and cast size are surface differences that some life games happen to have but that are not the criterion.
explanation.direct: Time horizon distinguishes a life game. Drama is a side effect of duration; cast size is incidental. The structural fact the chapter is built on is the multi-year scale.
explanation.competitive: Years, not minutes. Years, not relationships. The other answers describe surface features of some life games but miss the structural criterion the chapter is built on.

questions.prompt: Greta is signing the fourth partnership agreement of her career and the previous three ended the same way. According to the chapter, what specifically is the pattern paying her?
choices: A series of bad-luck stories to tell at parties
Practice in choosing better business partners

A confirmation of a position she has been holding since her twenties (the world will take what it can take from me) plus the small reliable strokes of being seen as the generous and put-upon one afterward

explanation.gentle: The chapter is specific. The pattern is paying Greta two reinforcing things: the position she has been holding since her twenties gets confirmed each time, and the small strokes of being seen as generous and put-upon afterward arrive on a schedule. The first wrong answer trivializes the payoff; the second moralizes it.
explanation.direct: Position confirmation plus reliable post-ending strokes is the structural answer. Calling the payoff 'bad-luck stories' trivializes it; calling it 'practice in better choices' moralizes it into a learning opportunity, which the chapter is explicit it is not.
explanation.competitive: Position and post-ending strokes. The other answers are the soft readings the chapter spends six paragraphs refusing. Greta is not collecting stories for parties and she is not learning to choose better partners. She is solving a structural problem with the only tool she has.

questions.prompt: Felix has been running a righteous-outrage pattern at his hospital department for twenty years, releasing stored procedural lapses as justified outrage when a colleague makes an unambiguous mistake. According to the chapter, what does the antithesis to this pattern require?
choices: A colleague who is so impeccable in their procedure that Felix's collection file stays empty, with the cost that the impeccable procedure takes unmeasured hours of the colleague's time
Confronting Felix about the pattern
A different department head

explanation.gentle: The chapter is explicit. The antithesis to the righteous-outrage pattern is impeccable procedure that gives Felix no opening, and the chapter is honest that the impeccability is expensive in time. Confronting Felix directly will provoke the next release. A different department head changes the player but not the pattern.
explanation.direct: Impeccable procedure, with the cost named honestly, is the chapter's structural answer. Confrontation provokes the release; changing the department head substitutes one player for another and does not address the pattern.
explanation.competitive: Impeccable procedure. Costs hours. Worth it. Confronting Felix is the move that runs the next instance of the pattern, and changing department heads is the move that pretends the pattern lived in one person.

questions.prompt: Ivar, a project coordinator, explains every mistake on every project as the consequence of a colleague who interrupted him at the critical moment. In the most recent instance, he blamed Zoe. What role is Zoe being cast in?
choices: The persecutor in a substance-pattern cast
The interrupting witness whose presence lets Ivar offload responsibility for a mistake that did not actually have anything to do with her
Felix's colleague in a different game

explanation.gentle: The chapter is structural here. Zoe is being cast as the interrupting witness whose presence lets Ivar offload the blame. The mistake had nothing to do with her. The first wrong answer borrows vocabulary from a different pattern; the third confuses two of the chapter's anchors.
explanation.direct: Interrupting witness is the role Ivar's pattern assigns to whoever was nearest. The chapter is explicit that the witness's actual involvement in the mistake is not the criterion. Persecutor vocabulary belongs to the substance pattern, which this chapter does not cover.
explanation.competitive: Witness, not persecutor, not Felix's colleague. The mistake had nothing to do with her. Her job in the script is to have been nearby. The other answers borrow from games this chapter is explicitly not running.

questions.prompt: Mona is a freelancer who has been taking on more work than she can complete at rates she cannot sustain for ten years. What does the chapter say the dynamics of her pattern are?
choices: She is bad at project management
She is unlucky in client selection

She needs the proof that nothing can be done about her situation, and the over-commit cycle reliably produces that proof on a schedule, with sympathy strokes from her closest friends as the secondary payoff

explanation.gentle: The chapter is structural about Mona. The dynamics are her need for the proof that nothing can be done, and the over-commit cycle is producing the proof on a schedule. The wrong answers both moralize the pattern as bad project management or bad luck, which the chapter explicitly refuses.
explanation.direct: Need for proof of impossibility plus reliable sympathy strokes is the chapter's structural answer. Project management and luck are the surface readings the chapter is built to refuse.
explanation.competitive: Proof of impossibility. Sympathy strokes. Both reliable, both on a schedule. The chapter spends multiple paragraphs refusing the project-management and luck readings, which are the comfortable answers and the wrong ones.

questions.prompt: Tomi is a high school junior running a rejection-inviting pattern in Mr. Wendell's history class: late, wrong tone with the wrong students, surprised hurt at the consequences. According to the chapter, which move is Wendell most likely to make WORSE the pattern with?
choices: Calling Tomi out directly in front of the class for the pattern, or punishing him with a detention
Giving Tomi a small specific responsibility in the next class period that has nothing to do with the pattern
Speaking with another teacher about the pattern privately

explanation.gentle: Direct confrontation and punishment both confirm the pattern, because the pattern is paying Tomi the sympathy strokes that follow each consequence.
